stem: Which clauses of ISO 9001 contain the auditable requirements?
options: Clauses 4 through 10.
Clauses 1 through 3.
Clauses 0 through 5.
Clauses 6 through 10 only.
rationale: The introductory clauses set scope and vocabulary; the requirements an auditor assesses are in the clauses on context through improvement.

stem: Who is accountable for the effectiveness of the QMS?
options: The quality manager alone.
The internal audit team.
The certification body.
Top management.
rationale: Top management retains accountability and demonstrates it through leadership, even when tasks are delegated.

stem: An operator is unsure whether a work instruction is the current revision. What is the best action?
options: Continue with the copy at the workstation, since it has been used before.
Use the revision that a colleague remembers as the latest.
Verify against the controlled document system or ask the supervisor before proceeding.
Proceed and correct the work later if a problem is found.
rationale: Documented information in use must be the current, controlled version; uncertainty is resolved before work continues.

stem: A measuring instrument or test tool shows that its calibration or verification date has passed. What should be done?
options: Use it carefully and note the overdue date on the record.
Do not use it; flag it out and notify the supervisor or the calibration owner.
Use it only for non-critical checks.
Adjust the date label to the next scheduled week.
rationale: Equipment past its calibration status cannot give valid results and must be withdrawn and reported.

stem: A measuring instrument is found out of tolerance at calibration. What must the organization evaluate?
options: Only the cost of recalibrating the instrument.
The validity of earlier measurements made with it and any affected outputs.
Whether the calibration laboratory used the correct label.
Only measurements taken after the calibration.
rationale: An out-of-tolerance finding casts doubt on previous results, so affected measurements and outputs must be assessed.

stem: Material, data, or equipment supplied by a customer for use in the work is best described as what?
options: Customer property that must be identified, protected, and reported if lost or damaged.
Free stock that may be used for any purpose.
Internal inventory once it has been received.
A provider output that needs no special care.
rationale: Property belonging to customers or external providers is safeguarded and any loss, damage, or unsuitability is reported to its owner.

stem: A work item fails a check and is about to be released to the customer. First action?
options: Release it and inform the customer afterward.
Quietly rework it and release it without a record.
Move it to the end of the queue for later review.
Stop the release, flag and hold the work item, and notify the supervisor and quality.
rationale: Nonconforming outputs must be identified and controlled to prevent unintended use or delivery.

stem: Which best defines a correction?
options: An action to remove the cause of a nonconformity.
A periodic review of quality objectives.
An action to deal with the nonconforming output itself.
A planned audit of a process.
rationale: A correction addresses the output at hand; removing the cause is corrective action.

stem: Which best defines a corrective action?
options: An action that repairs the single affected work item.
An action that records the problem in a log.
An action to eliminate the cause so the nonconformity does not recur.
An action that informs the customer of the problem.
rationale: Corrective action targets cause, not only the immediate symptom.

stem: Root cause analysis concludes "operator error." What is the best next step?
options: Close the investigation and retrain the individual.
Ask why the system allowed the error (instruction, training, tooling, workload, design).
Reassign the operator to other duties.
Record it as a one-off and take no action.
rationale: Human error is usually a symptom; the system conditions that permitted it need examination.

stem: Why are training records retained?
options: They are evidence of competence.
They are required only for new employees.
They replace the need for performance observation.
They list the cost of each course.
rationale: Retained information on education, training, skills, and experience demonstrates that people are competent.

stem: An internal auditor audits his own department's work. What is the concern?
options: The audit will take longer than planned.
The department may lack a documented procedure.
The auditor will not be familiar with the process.
Lack of objectivity and impartiality.
rationale: Auditors must not assess their own work, so that results are objective and impartial.

stem: Which is a required input to management review?
options: Individual payroll details.
The personal preferences of the auditor.
The marketing budget for the year.
Customer satisfaction and feedback trends (among others listed in the standard).
rationale: Management review considers performance information, including customer feedback, alongside other defined inputs.

stem: A process parameter will be changed. What must happen before implementation?
options: Inform the operators on the next shift.
Test the change on live work and keep it if results look fine.
Review the change and its consequences, and obtain authorization, with records.
Wait for a customer complaint before deciding.
rationale: Changes are planned and reviewed for their effects, and authorized, so continued conformity is not compromised.

stem: A provider changes a material specification, software version, or method and notifies the organization. What is appropriate?
options: Accept it automatically because the provider is approved.
Evaluate the change and its effect on the process and output before acceptance.
Ignore the notice until a nonconformity appears.
Reject all changes from providers as a rule.
rationale: Externally provided processes, products, and services must continue to meet requirements, so changes are evaluated before use.

stem: An order arrives with a changed specification. What must occur before processing?
options: Review the requirement change and confirm the company can meet it; inform affected people.
Process it as usual and update the paperwork later.
Wait for the customer to confirm receipt of the original.
Pass the change only to the sales team.
rationale: Changed requirements are reviewed for capability and communicated so relevant persons are aware.

stem: An auditor asks a question you cannot answer. What is the best response?
options: State that you do not know and will find out, then refer to the supervisor; do not guess.
Give the most likely answer to avoid delay.
Change the subject to a process you know well.
Ask the auditor to come back after the audit.
rationale: Honest answers and prompt referral preserve the integrity of the evidence; speculation can mislead.

stem: Which statement about risk-based thinking is correct?
options: A formal risk register is mandatory for every process.
Risk-based thinking applies only to safety hazards.
Risk actions must eliminate every risk.
Actions should be proportionate to potential impact on conformity; formal risk methods are not mandated.
rationale: Planning actions address risks and opportunities in proportion to their possible effect, without prescribing a particular method.

stem: Which best describes a quality objective?
options: A general statement of company values.
A list of all procedures in use.
A measurable aim consistent with the policy and relevant to conformity and customer satisfaction.
A one-time inspection target set by the auditor.
rationale: Objectives are measurable, monitored, and aligned with the policy and with customer satisfaction.

stem: A work item is released while a final check discrepancy is open, without approval. Which requirement is breached?
options: Customer communication requirements.
Release controls; release requires satisfactory completion of arrangements or authorized approval.
Management review scheduling.
Design input requirements.
rationale: Release must wait until planned checks are complete, unless an authorized person approves otherwise.

stem: Records are completed at the end of shift from memory. What is the primary risk?
options: The records may be too detailed.
Inaccurate records that cannot serve as objective evidence.
The shift will finish later than planned.
The records may be stored in the wrong format.
rationale: Records must be reliable to demonstrate conformity; recollection introduces errors and gaps.

stem: A hold flag is removed and the work item is reworked without disposition. What is the issue?
options: Unauthorized handling of nonconforming output; disposition and authority were not documented.
Rework is never permitted for any output.
The flag should have been a different color.
Nothing, if the rework was successful.
rationale: Nonconforming outputs are dealt with under a recorded disposition by someone with authority.

stem: Which is evidence of traceability?
options: A general statement that all work is controlled.
The quality policy displayed in the work area.
A list of approved providers.
Records linking a work item to its inputs, equipment or systems, process steps, and people.
rationale: Traceability depends on unique identification and records that connect the output to what was used and done.

stem: What is the purpose of an effectiveness check on corrective action?
options: Confirm that the form was completed on time.
Assign blame to the responsible person.
Confirm that the cause was eliminated and the problem did not recur.
Reduce the number of audits.
rationale: Reviewing effectiveness shows whether the action actually worked.

stem: A controlled work environment condition (for example temperature, cleanliness, system availability, or staffing) moves outside its limits. Which clause area addresses the environment?
options: Customer property.
Management review.
Environment for the operation of processes.
Design and development outputs.
rationale: The organization determines, provides, and maintains the environment needed for processes to produce conforming output.

stem: Who is responsible for knowing the quality policy?
options: Only top management.
Everyone, to the extent it relates to their work.
Only the quality department.
Only people who interact with customers.
rationale: Persons doing work under the organization's control must be aware of the policy and how they contribute.

stem: Which is a valid reason for an operator to stop a process?
options: Evidence that the process is producing nonconforming product, subject to defined authority.
The operator would prefer an earlier break.
A colleague disagrees with the schedule.
The work is more difficult than usual.
rationale: Defined responsibilities and authorities allow people to halt work that is generating nonconforming output.

stem: Can the company keep a documented quality manual?
options: No; a manual is prohibited by the standard.
Yes, and it is mandatory for every organization.
Only if a certification body requests it.
Yes; a manual is not mandatory under the 2015 edition but many companies retain one.
rationale: The 2015 edition leaves the extent of documented information to the organization.

stem: Which is a correct description of an audit finding?
options: An auditor's opinion of a person's performance.
A suggestion for how to redesign the process.
A summary of the auditee's complaints.
A statement based on objective evidence referencing the requirement not met.
rationale: Findings rest on verifiable evidence tied to a specific requirement.

stem: What distinguishes a concession from a correction?
options: A concession is a type of audit; a correction is a record.
A concession is always rejected; a correction is optional.
A concession is authorized acceptance of nonconforming output; a correction removes or fixes the nonconformity.
They have the same meaning.
rationale: A concession accepts output as is under authority; a correction changes the output or situation to resolve the nonconformity.

stem: Which activity best illustrates the organization determining its context?
options: Printing the list of current work instructions.
Reviewing external and internal issues that affect its ability to achieve intended results.
Counting the number of calibrated instruments.
Scheduling the annual audit calendar.
rationale: Understanding context means identifying issues relevant to purpose and strategic direction.

stem: A supervisor learns that a new regulation will affect how a process is carried out. Which clause area is most directly engaged?
options: Understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties.
Calibration of monitoring equipment.
Internal audit independence.
Control of customer property.
rationale: Applicable statutory and regulatory expectations are inputs to what the QMS must address.

stem: Which is an example of an interested party relevant to the QMS?
options: A customer or external provider whose requirements affect conformity.
Only the owners of the company.
Only the certification body.
Only employees in the quality department.
rationale: Interested parties are those that can affect or be affected by the organization's ability to deliver conforming outputs.

stem: What does the scope of the QMS state?
options: The names of all employees.
The target selling price of each product.
The schedule of management meetings.
The boundaries and applicability of the system, including products and services covered.
rationale: The scope is maintained as documented information and defines where the system applies.

stem: A team proposes excluding a requirement from the QMS because it seems inconvenient. What is the correct view?
options: Any requirement may be excluded if management agrees.
Exclusions are never allowed under any circumstances.
An exclusion is acceptable only if the requirement is not applicable and it does not affect conformity of outputs.
Exclusions are allowed if the auditor is not told.
rationale: Non-applicability must be genuine and must not undermine assurance of conforming output or customer satisfaction.

stem: What is the purpose of a process approach in the QMS?
options: To assign every task to a separate department.
To manage interacting activities as processes with defined inputs, outputs, and responsibilities.
To replace measurement with observation.
To remove the need for records.
rationale: Treating work as interrelated processes allows consistent management of results.

stem: An operator notices that the output of an upstream step regularly arrives incomplete. Which idea best explains why this matters?
options: Each step is independent and only its own results count.
Processes interact, so the output of one step is the input of the next and must meet its needs.
Incomplete inputs are acceptable if the downstream step is faster.
Only the final inspection is accountable.
rationale: Process interaction means problems pass downstream unless inputs are defined and controlled.

stem: Which is typically a defined element when describing a process?
options: Inputs, outputs, resources, responsibilities, and performance indicators.
The private opinions of the process owner.
The seniority of the staff member.
The color of the forms used.
rationale: Determining inputs, outputs, sequence, criteria, resources, and responsibilities supports effective process control.

stem: Which of these demonstrates top management leadership of the QMS?
options: Performing all internal audits personally.
Delegating every quality matter without follow-up.
Approving each work instruction individually.
Ensuring the policy and objectives are established and aligned with strategic direction.
rationale: Leadership involves direction, integration of requirements into business processes, and provision of resources.

stem: A manager repeatedly instructs teams to meet delivery dates even when checks are incomplete. What does this undermine?
options: The physical layout of the facility.
The color-coding of tooling.
A culture that supports quality and customer focus.
The calibration schedule.
rationale: Leadership messages and priorities shape whether people follow quality requirements under pressure.

stem: How is customer focus demonstrated by top management?
options: By offering discounts on every order.
By reducing the number of customer contacts.
By ensuring customer and applicable statutory requirements are determined and consistently met.
By limiting complaints to a single channel.
rationale: Customer focus requires that risks and opportunities affecting conformity and satisfaction are addressed.

stem: Which statement about the quality policy is correct?
options: It is confidential and held only by management.
It must be available, communicated, and understood within the organization and available to relevant interested parties as appropriate.
It is replaced each month.
It applies only to the sales function.
rationale: The policy is documented, communicated, and kept available.

stem: What must a quality policy include a commitment to?
options: Satisfying applicable requirements and continually improving the QMS.
Reducing headcount each year.
Lowering the price of all products.
Eliminating every possible risk.
rationale: Policy commitments cover applicable requirements and continual improvement, and provide a framework for objectives.

stem: Why must responsibilities and authorities be assigned and communicated?
options: So that only managers may speak to auditors.
So that job titles can be standardized.
So that records need not be maintained.
So that everyone knows who is accountable for process results and who may act when something goes wrong.
rationale: Clear roles ensure the QMS conforms and that issues are reported and acted upon.

stem: During a shift, a technician sees a process drifting toward limits but no one is assigned to decide on stopping it. What gap does this show?
options: The calibration schedule is too frequent.
The audit program is too large.
The customer survey is out of date.
Responsibility and authority for process decisions were not clearly assigned or communicated.
rationale: Defined authority lets people act promptly to protect conformity.

stem: Who should be assigned responsibility for reporting QMS performance to top management?
options: Any visitor to the site.
Only the external auditor.
A person with defined responsibility and authority for this reporting.
No one; reports are optional.
rationale: Top management assigns responsibility for reporting on performance and for ensuring the system remains conforming.

stem: What does the organization consider when planning the QMS?
options: Only financial risks.
Risks and opportunities that need to be addressed to give assurance of results.
Only risks that have already occurred.
Only risks identified by customers.
rationale: Planning identifies what could affect the intended results and what could enhance them.

stem: A supervisor identifies that a single trained person performs a critical step. Which response reflects risk-based thinking?
options: Plan a proportionate action, such as cross-training, to reduce dependence on one person.
Take no action until the person leaves.
Prepare a formal risk register for the entire company.
Ask the person to work additional hours.
rationale: Actions are proportionate to the potential effect on conformity of outputs.

stem: Which is a characteristic of a well-formed quality objective?
options: It is measurable, monitored, communicated, and updated as appropriate.
It is vague and long term only.
It is set by an external body.
It never changes.
rationale: Objectives are measurable where practicable and monitored.

stem: When setting an objective, which question must be answered in planning how to achieve it?
options: Which supplier is the cheapest.
Who wrote the policy.
Which audit is next.
What will be done, what resources are needed, who is responsible, when it will be finished, and how results will be evaluated.
rationale: Planning to achieve objectives defines actions, resources, responsibility, timing, and evaluation.

stem: A team wants to alter the sequence of a process to save time. What must be considered?
options: Only whether the new sequence is faster.
Only the opinion of the most senior person.
The purpose of the change, its potential consequences, resources, and responsibilities.
Nothing, if the change is temporary.
rationale: Changes to the QMS are carried out in a planned manner so integrity of the system is maintained.

stem: Which is an example of an opportunity in the planning sense?
options: A nonconformity found in an audit.
A chance to improve a process or adopt a new method that enhances results.
A complaint from a customer.
A missed delivery.
rationale: Opportunities are favorable circumstances that can improve performance.

stem: An operator suggests a better way to stage tools that would reduce handling errors. How is this best treated?
options: As criticism of the supervisor that should be ignored.
As an improvement opportunity to be reviewed and, if suitable, introduced through planned change.
As something to implement immediately without review.
As a matter only for the quality manager.
rationale: Ideas are channelled through review and change planning so integrity is preserved.

stem: What kinds of resources must the organization provide for the QMS?
options: People, infrastructure, an environment for operation, monitoring and measuring resources, and knowledge.
Only people and money.
Only equipment.
Only documented procedures.
rationale: Resource provision spans several categories needed to operate and control processes.

stem: Which is the best example of infrastructure needed for conformity?
options: The quality policy statement.
The annual audit report.
The customer complaint log.
Buildings, equipment, software, and supporting services such as transport or communication.
rationale: Infrastructure covers physical and technical facilities that processes depend on.

stem: A shared software tool crashes repeatedly and delays checks. What should be recognized?
options: Software problems are outside the QMS.
Only customers should be informed.
Infrastructure must be maintained so that conforming output is not put at risk.
Delays are acceptable if outputs are correct.
rationale: Provision and maintenance of infrastructure is part of operating the system.

stem: What must be done to confirm that measurement results are valid when traceability is required?
options: Use the instrument until it fails.
Rely on the operator's judgment.
Calibrate or verify equipment against standards traceable to recognized references, and identify its status.
Repair it only after complaints.
rationale: Valid, traceable results depend on calibration or verification at defined intervals.

stem: Why does the organization manage organizational knowledge?
options: To avoid having to train anyone.
To have the knowledge necessary for process operation and conformity, and to keep it available.
To keep it secret from auditors.
To replace the need for records.
rationale: Knowledge from experience and lessons learned must be maintained and available.

stem: A highly experienced technician is retiring. Which action best addresses the QMS requirement on knowledge?
options: Capture and transfer the technician's know-how to others before departure.
Wait until a problem emerges.
Rely on the technician's memory after they leave.
Remove the process from the scope.
rationale: Knowledge held by individuals is a resource at risk if not captured.

stem: How does the organization demonstrate competence?
options: By hiring only senior staff.
By limiting access to work areas.
By publishing job titles.
By determining needed competence, ensuring people have it, taking action where gaps exist, and retaining evidence.
rationale: Competence is determined, assured, evaluated, and evidenced.

stem: A new operator has completed a classroom session but has not yet performed the task. What should the supervisor do?
options: Assume competence because the session was attended.
Record the person as competent immediately.
Assign the task and check only if a problem arises.
Confirm competence through observation or assessment before assigning independent work.
rationale: Attendance alone does not prove competence; effectiveness of training is evaluated.

stem: Which statement describes awareness under the QMS?
options: People can recite the standard.
People know only their job title.
People are aware of the policy, relevant objectives, their contribution, and the implications of not conforming.
People are aware only of customer names.
rationale: Awareness links personal work to the system and its results.

stem: During an audit, an operator is asked how their work affects quality objectives. What does this test?
options: The operator's financial knowledge.
Awareness of how personal work contributes to the QMS and its objectives.
The operator's seniority.
The calibration status of tools.
rationale: Auditors confirm that people understand their contribution.

stem: Which describes communication requirements within the QMS?
options: The organization determines what, when, with whom, how, and who will communicate on matters relevant to the QMS.
All information is shared with all parties at all times.
Communication is verbal only.
Only management communicates.
rationale: Internal and external communication is planned around relevant needs.

stem: A shift ends and the incoming team is not told that a work item is on hold. Which area has failed?
options: Internal communication about matters relevant to the QMS.
Calibration traceability.
Management review inputs.
Corrective action effectiveness.
rationale: Relevant status must be communicated so that held items are not released or processed in error.

stem: Which information typically needs documented control?
options: Every email sent.
Only information requested by customers.
Only information on paper.
Information required by the QMS and determined by the organization as necessary for effectiveness.
rationale: The extent of documented information depends on size, complexity, processes, and competence.

stem: Which is needed when creating or updating documented information?
options: Only the author's initials.
Only the printed date.
Appropriate identification, format, and review and approval for suitability and adequacy.
No review if the change is small.
rationale: Creation and updating require controls that keep documents suitable and identifiable.

stem: Which control helps prevent unintended use of obsolete documented information?
options: Leaving it in the work area for reference.
Removing it from points of use or identifying it clearly if retained for any purpose.
Storing it in a personal drawer.
Letting each person decide.
rationale: Distribution, access, storage, and control of changes protect against use of superseded content.

stem: An operator finds an old printed instruction stapled to a machine that differs from the current version. What is the right action?
options: Leave it, since people know which to follow.
Remove or flag it and report it so that only the current version is available at the point of use.
Update it by hand with pen.
Photograph it and ignore it.
rationale: Obsolete content at the point of use is a risk to conformity.

stem: Why is a record not changed after the event with different ink or an unmarked overwrite?
options: Records provide evidence, so corrections must be traceable and protected from alteration.
Records have no legal value.
Ink color is mandated.
Records may only be written once per year.
rationale: Records are protected from unintended alteration and loss.

stem: What does operational planning and control require?
options: Only inspecting finished output.
Waiting for customers to specify methods.
Delegating all control to providers.
Planning, implementing, and controlling the processes needed to meet requirements for products and services.
rationale: Operational planning defines requirements, criteria, resources, and records.

stem: An unexpected staff shortage changes how a process must be run for two weeks. What does operational planning and control expect?
options: Ignore the shortage because it is temporary.
Stop all work for two weeks.
Review the consequences and take action to mitigate adverse effects on conformity.
Shorten checks to match the available time.
rationale: The consequences of unintended changes are reviewed and action is taken to mitigate any adverse effects on conformity.

stem: Which must be determined in communicating with customers?
options: The private contact details of all staff.
Only price changes.
Information about products and services, handling enquiries and orders, feedback, and customer property.
Only complaints.
rationale: Customer communication includes enquiries, contracts, feedback, and special requirements.

stem: When a customer verbally places an order without a written record, what should happen?
options: The order is processed from memory.
The requirements are confirmed before acceptance.
The order is rejected automatically.
The order is processed first and confirmed later.
rationale: If the customer provides no documented statement, requirements are confirmed before acceptance.

stem: Which is part of reviewing requirements for products and services?
options: Confirming the organization can meet requirements before committing to supply.
Setting a delivery date regardless of capacity.
Delaying all reviews until after delivery.
Waiting until the customer complains.
rationale: Capability is confirmed before commitment.

stem: Which statement best fits design and development controls?
options: Design is the sole responsibility of one person.
Verification is optional.
Changes are never recorded.
Reviews, verification, and validation are carried out at planned stages to confirm requirements are met.
rationale: Design controls include review, verification, validation, and control of changes.

stem: A design change is requested late in the project. What must be done?
options: Apply it quietly to meet the date.
Ignore the change since it is late.
Delay recording until completion.
Identify, review, and control the change, and retain information on the review and authorization.
rationale: Design changes are controlled to prevent adverse effects on conformity.

stem: Why does an organization evaluate and select external providers?
options: To reduce the number of records.
To avoid communication with providers.
To ensure externally provided processes, products, and services conform to requirements.
To increase the number of suppliers.
rationale: Criteria for evaluation, selection, monitoring, and re-evaluation are applied.

stem: A provider delivers material that does not match the purchase requirements. What is appropriate?
options: Use it, since it was delivered.
Treat it as nonconforming, hold it, and notify the provider as defined by the process.
Return it silently.
Mix it with approved stock.
rationale: Verification of provided items prevents incorrect material from entering the process.

stem: What must the organization communicate to external providers?
options: The requirements for the processes, products, and services, competence, and verification activities.
Only the delivery date.
Internal employee names.
Only the price.
rationale: Providers need adequate information to supply conforming outputs.

stem: Which is a characteristic of controlled conditions for production and service provision?
options: Availability of information defining characteristics, suitable resources, monitoring, and use of suitable infrastructure.
Reliance on operator memory.
Absence of checks.
Informal instructions only.
rationale: Controlled conditions give confidence that results conform.

stem: When is identification of outputs required?
options: Only at the end of a process.
Only when a customer asks.
Never.
When necessary to ensure conformity, outputs are identified by suitable means throughout production.
rationale: Identification supports status and traceability.

stem: Two work items of different status look identical and are placed in the same container. What control is lacking?
options: Customer property control.
Management review.
Identification of status with respect to monitoring and measurement requirements.
Design verification.
rationale: Status identification prevents mix-ups between conforming and nonconforming outputs.

stem: A work item owned by the customer is damaged while stored. What should be done?
options: Repair it quietly and return it.
Report it to the customer and retain a record of what occurred.
Replace it without telling the customer.
Scrap it.
rationale: Loss, damage, or unsuitability of customer property is reported to the owner.

stem: Which supports preservation of outputs during processing?
options: Leaving items exposed.
Appropriate handling, packaging, storage, and protection.
Storing items wherever space is free.
Using unlabelled containers.
rationale: Preservation includes identification, handling, contamination control, packaging, storage, and transmission.

stem: After delivery, a customer reports a fault that falls under a service obligation. What does the organization need to consider?
options: Post-delivery activities required, including warranty obligations, feedback, and customer requirements.
Only the next order.
Nothing, once delivered.
Only the invoice.
rationale: Post-delivery requirements are determined and met.

stem: What is required when changes to production or service provision occur?
options: Informal agreement between operators.
No review if the change is minor.
Changes only after complaints.
Review and control to ensure continuing conformity, with documented results and authorization.
rationale: Changes are reviewed and controlled to maintain conformity.

stem: Which is required before releasing products and services to the customer?
options: Releasing first and inspecting later.
Skipping checks when schedules are tight.
Implementing planned arrangements at appropriate stages to verify requirements are met.
Relying on customer inspection.
rationale: Release follows satisfactory completion of arrangements, unless approved by an authority and, where applicable, the customer.

stem: What information is retained about release?
options: Only the delivery address.
Only the invoice number.
Evidence of conformity with acceptance criteria and traceability to the persons authorizing release.
The staff roster.
rationale: Records show who authorized release and against what criteria.

stem: Which is a possible disposition of nonconforming output?
options: Ignoring it if no one noticed.
Correction, segregation, containment, return, suspension of provision, or acceptance under concession.
Mixing it with conforming items.
Releasing it with a note.
rationale: Nonconforming output is handled according to its nature and effect, with conformity verified after correction.

stem: After a nonconforming work item is reworked, what must happen before it is used?
options: Conformity is verified again and records of the disposition are retained.
It is released since rework is complete.
It is accepted on the operator's word.
It is returned to the line without a check.
rationale: Corrected outputs are re-verified.

stem: Nonconforming output is detected after delivery. What is appropriate?
options: Wait for the customer to detect it.
Alter the records.
Do nothing if the item has been used.
Take action appropriate to the effects, including informing the customer.
rationale: Action addresses the actual or potential effects.

stem: Which information must be retained for nonconformities?
options: Only the date.
Only the operator's name.
Only the customer's name.
The description, actions taken, concessions obtained, and the authority deciding the action.
rationale: Records describe the nonconformity and how it was dealt with.

stem: A repeated minor defect is reworked each time but never reported. What is the weakness?
options: Rework is not allowed.
Reports are only for major defects.
The cause is never identified, so the nonconformity is likely to recur.
The defect must be hidden.
rationale: Reporting enables analysis and corrective action.

stem: What does the organization monitor, measure, analyze, and evaluate?
options: Only financial performance.
What needs to be monitored and measured, the methods, when, and when to analyze and evaluate the results.
Only audits.
Only complaints.
rationale: Performance evaluation is planned to check effectiveness of the QMS.

stem: Why is customer satisfaction monitored?
options: To determine the degree to which customer needs and expectations have been fulfilled.
To identify who to blame.
To reduce the number of customers.
Only to satisfy auditors.
rationale: Perception of the customer is monitored through suitable methods.

stem: A customer survey shows declining satisfaction on delivery. What is the best response?
options: Analyze the data and use it to inform actions and management review.
Ignore the survey.
Change the survey questions.
Remove the delivery metric.
rationale: Analysis of data supports improvement.

stem: Which is an output of analysis and evaluation?
options: Only a list of staff.
Only audit schedules.
Only invoices.
Information on conformity, customer satisfaction, process performance, provider performance, and improvement needs.
rationale: Analysis results inform decisions on QMS performance and improvement.

stem: Why are internal audits performed?
options: To find staff to discipline.
To replace management review.
To provide information on whether the QMS conforms and is effectively implemented and maintained.
To satisfy a customer's request only.
rationale: Audits check conformity to organization and standard requirements.

stem: Which is required of an audit program?
options: Auditing only easy areas.
Planning that considers importance of processes, changes, and results of previous audits.
Auditing only once in total.
Avoiding follow-up.
rationale: The program is planned with frequency, methods, responsibilities, and criteria.

stem: An audit finds a nonconformity. What follows?
options: Wait until the next audit.
Correction and corrective action without undue delay, with results reported to relevant management.
Close it without action.
Remove the auditor.
rationale: Findings are acted on and records retained.

stem: How often must management review take place?
options: At planned intervals determined by the organization.
Only after a complaint.
Never.
Only in the first year.
rationale: Reviews are at planned intervals to ensure continuing suitability, adequacy, effectiveness, and alignment.

stem: Which is a required output of management review?
options: Only a list of attendees.
Only the next audit date.
Only the minutes of the last meeting.
Decisions and actions on improvement, any need for QMS changes, and resource needs.
rationale: Outputs drive improvement and resourcing.

stem: A manager proposes skipping management review because performance appears fine. What is the issue?
options: Reviews are optional.
Only poor performance needs review.
Review is required at planned intervals regardless of how performance appears.
Only customers decide.
rationale: Planned review confirms continuing suitability and effectiveness.

stem: An operator records a measurement of an item but is unsure whether it passed. What is the right step?
options: Mark it as passed.
Leave the field blank.
Check against defined acceptance criteria or ask for guidance before recording or releasing.
Record it as failed without check.
rationale: Acceptance criteria define the pass or fail decision.

stem: What is the purpose of continual improvement?
options: To reduce all costs.
To enhance the suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness of the QMS.
To remove audits.
To change the policy every month.
rationale: The organization uses analysis, review outputs, and opportunities to improve.

stem: A team proposes an improvement from analysis results. Which clause area does this fall under?
options: Improvement, including responding to needs and opportunities.
Customer property.
Document control.
Identification.
rationale: Improvement actions are selected from analysis and review outputs.

stem: A nonconformity occurs. What must the organization do first?
options: Wait for management review.
Hide the evidence.
Wait for an audit.
React to it and, as applicable, take action to control and correct it and deal with consequences.
rationale: Reaction includes control, correction, and addressing consequences.

stem: Which step in corrective action evaluates the need to eliminate causes?
options: Writing a report only.
Closing the record immediately.
Retraining without analysis.
Reviewing and analyzing the nonconformity and determining its causes and whether similar ones exist.
rationale: Cause analysis decides whether similar nonconformities exist or could occur.

stem: After implementing a corrective action, what must be reviewed?
options: The color of the form.
The number of pages.
The effectiveness of the action taken.
The author's title.
rationale: Effectiveness is reviewed and records are retained.

stem: What records are retained for corrective action?
options: Only the closing date.
The nature of nonconformities, actions taken, and the results of those actions.
Only the audit name.
Only the supervisor's name.
rationale: Documented information is retained as evidence.

stem: A problem is closed after a one-time fix, and it recurs three weeks later. What was likely missing?
options: Cause analysis and an effectiveness check.
Calibration records.
A new logo.
Customer approval.
rationale: Without cause elimination and verification, recurrence is likely.

stem: Which input might feed continual improvement?
options: Results of analysis and evaluation and outputs from management review.
Staff birthdays.
Parking permits.
Office layout alone.
rationale: Analysis and review outputs identify underperformance and opportunities.

stem: During an audit, an operator volunteers information not asked for about a different process. What is the better practice?
options: Speak at length about all topics.
Refuse to answer anything.
Guess to fill gaps.
Answer the question asked, honestly and concisely, without speculation.
rationale: Clear, factual answers keep the audit focused on evidence.

stem: Why might an auditor ask to see records for a work item at random?
options: To catch someone out.
To waste time.
To sample objective evidence of conformity.
To rewrite the records.
rationale: Auditors sample evidence to verify implementation.

stem: An auditor asks to observe you performing a task. What is the correct approach?
options: Work faster than usual.
Work normally, following the current instruction.
Skip steps for the demonstration.
Refuse, citing a busy schedule.
rationale: The audit samples normal practice against requirements.

stem: An auditor raises an observation rather than a nonconformity. What does this indicate?
options: A formal failure of the QMS.
A potential issue or improvement opportunity, not a failure to meet a requirement.
A reason to end the audit.
A legal violation.
rationale: Observations note potential concerns; nonconformities cite unmet requirements.

stem: A supervisor notices that records for an inspection step are routinely left blank by the team. Which is the most appropriate response?
options: Treat it as a gap in control of records, correct the practice, and investigate the cause.
Ignore it if outputs look fine.
Fill in the records for the team later.
Remove the inspection step.
rationale: Missing records mean there is no evidence of conformity, which needs correction and cause analysis.

stem: A technician is asked by a colleague to sign off a check not witnessed. What should the technician do?
options: Sign it to save time.
Sign it and add a note later.
Ask another colleague to sign.
Decline and explain that records must reflect actual verification.
rationale: Records that misstate verification undermine evidence and integrity.

stem: A work item at the final check shows a characteristic marginally outside acceptance criteria. The customer is waiting. What is appropriate?
options: Release it to meet the deadline.
Adjust the criteria locally.
Hold it and seek an authorized disposition, which may include a concession from the customer.
Re-measure until it passes.
rationale: Only authorized acceptance can allow nonconforming output to be used.
